**Verdict: LEGAL.** Marcus Ibarra at $4,619,983 sits at or below the $9,096,000 threshold, so you get the widest matching band there is — 200% plus $250,000, or $9,489,966 — and Nikola Whitfield at $7,531,195 fits inside it with margin. The consequence is the part that needs your attention: taking back more salary than you send out hard-caps Atlanta at the first apron, $209,015,000, for the balance of the league year. You move from $202,025,582 to $204,936,794, leaving $4,078,206 under that ceiling, and it has to cover the 15th roster spot, in-season replacements and anything you want to do at the deadline. Workable, but genuinely tight. I would sign off only if Whitfield is a rotation upgrade rather than depth, because turning a small salary into a bigger one is the most expensive way to acquire a bench player when the price is a hard cap you keep all season.

You need to shed $8,393,011 — the distance from your apron salary of $216,217,011 to the second apron at $207,824,000 — and the cruel part is that sitting over the second apron already strips the tools you would normally use to get back under it. You cannot aggregate salaries in a trade and you cannot send cash, so this has to be done with single contracts moving out, one at a time. Four players clear the gap by themselves, assuming nothing comes back: Elijah Amadi at $15,107,837 clears it with $6,714,826 to spare, Andre Brantley at $22,422,161 with $14,029,150, Nico Nakamura at $22,915,305 with $14,522,294, and Nico Achiuwa at $27,466,600 with $19,073,589. Amadi is the cheapest route to compliance and the least damaging on the floor; the three larger contracts overshoot, which only helps if you also want tax relief or a reset below the first apron. The cost is the same in kind across all four — you are a forced seller against a deadline, the market knows it, and you will most likely attach a pick to move the salary with nothing coming back. Start those conversations early rather than at the buzzer.

$15,642,293 is what you owe, on $9,676,739 of payroll above the line. Tax salary is $180,490,739 against the 2024-25 threshold of $170,814,000. The first $5,168,000 of the overage bills at $1.50 per dollar, or $7,752,000; the remaining $4,508,739 crosses into the second bracket at $1.75 per dollar, or $7,890,293 — note that the second bracket costs more than the first while covering less payroll, which is the entire design of the schedule. You are on the standard rates rather than the repeater schedule, and that is worth protecting: paying the tax in three of any four seasons moves you onto repeater rates, where an identical payroll costs substantially more. Practical consequence for this summer — you have 13 players and two spots to fill, and every minimum contract you add is priced at the second-bracket rate, so budget the tax cost of roster-filling alongside the salary.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The exception itself is fine — $4,958,308 fits inside the taxpayer mid-level maximum of $5,685,000, leaving $726,692 unused. The problem is what invoking it does to you. The taxpayer mid-level hard-caps a team at the second apron, $207,824,000, and New Orleans already sits at $206,039,974. Add Cam Whitfield and you are at $210,998,282, which is $3,174,282 above a ceiling you would have just imposed on yourself. That is the trap with this exception: it is available at your apron level, but at your payroll it is unusable, because the act of using it creates the hard cap that the signing immediately violates. Two ways forward. Sign him to a minimum contract, which triggers no hard cap at all, or shed salary first so the taxpayer mid-level has somewhere to land — and if you go the second route, remember the hard cap attaches on the day you use the exception, so the salary has to be gone before the signing, not after.
